stem: Under Article X, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution, how long is one term of office of an elected municipal mayor?
hints: Local officials such as mayors, governors and councilors have their own term in Article X, separate from Members of Congress.
Article X, Section 8 sets one term length for all elective local officials except barangay officials.
Section 8 uses the same number twice: once for the years in one term, and once for the most consecutive terms allowed. Find that number and match it to the choices.

solution.methodName: Line up the ages and terms by office

steps.action: Find the rule: "The term of office of elective local officials, except barangay officials, which shall be determined by law, shall be three years."
steps.why: A mayor is an elective local official. Barangay officials are the only exception; their term is set by law.

steps.action: Note the limit: no such official "shall serve for more than three consecutive terms."
steps.why: Consecutive means one right after another. So a mayor may serve at most three terms in a row, or nine years.

steps.action: Note that voluntarily giving up the office does not break the run of terms.
steps.why: Voluntary renunciation of the office "for any length of time" does not count as a break in the official's service for the full term.

steps.action: One term of an elected municipal mayor is three years.

trapNotes.Two years: Section 8 gives no two-year term. Elective local officials, except barangay officials, serve three years.
trapNotes.Six years: Six years is the term of a Senator (Article VI, Section 4) and of the President (Article VII, Section 4), not of a local official.
trapNotes.Four years: Section 8 gives no four-year term. Elective local officials, except barangay officials, serve three years.
